blocks.text: Why the Ken Burns effect causes delays

The Ken Burns effect requires precise keyframe management. When you apply this to dozens of photos, you often face inconsistencies. If you do not have a standard preset, you must manually adjust the start and end positions for every single clip. This repetitive work is why many editors find the process laborious. It is a classic example of a task that feels small but consumes hours of your week.
Managing VFX complexity on your Mac

High resolution files like 4K or 6K footage often push your Mac to its limit. When you add complex visual effects on top of these files, software crashes become common. To avoid this, use optimized media or proxy files during your edit. Final Cut Pro handles this well with its background rendering features. DaVinci Resolve offers a more robust Fusion tab for complex VFX work, though it has a steeper learning curve. Always check your system resources in Activity Monitor by pressing ⌘ Space and typing Activity Monitor to ensure you are not overloading your CPU.
Fixes anyone can use for free

items: Create a master preset for your Ken Burns effect and save it as a custom transition or effect style.
Use keyboard shortcuts to jump between edit points instead of clicking with your mouse.
Organize your assets in Finder using tags before you import them into your editing software.
Keep your projects on a fast external SSD to reduce load times for high resolution assets.
Close unnecessary browser tabs in Chrome to free up RAM while you are rendering.
